history.heading: Kingdoms of the Congo River
paragraphs: The Republic of the Congo, often called Congo-Brazzaville to distinguish it from its larger neighbour, lies on the north bank of the Congo River. The region was home to the Kingdom of Loango on the coast, the Teke Kingdom inland, and parts of the Kingdom of Kongo. From the 16th century the coast became involved in the Atlantic slave trade.

history.heading: French Congo
paragraphs: The explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza signed a treaty with the Teke king in 1880, establishing French control, and Brazzaville was named after him. Concession companies exploited the region brutally for rubber and ivory. The Congo-Ocean railway, built in the 1920s and 1930s, cost many thousands of forced labourers their lives. Brazzaville was the capital of French Equatorial Africa and of Free France during the Second World War.

history.heading: Independence
paragraphs: Congo became independent on 15 August 1960. In 1969 it became the People's Republic of the Congo, Africa's first self-declared Marxist-Leninist state. Multiparty politics returned in 1991, but civil wars broke out in the 1990s, especially in 1997, when Denis Sassou Nguesso, who had ruled from 1979 to 1992, regained power with Angolan support. He has ruled ever since.

culture.heading: Music and fashion
paragraphs: French is the official language, and Lingala and Kituba are national languages. Most people are Christian. Brazzaville and Kinshasa face each other across the Congo River, sharing a rich musical culture of Congolese rumba, recognised by UNESCO, and soukous.
La Sape, a subculture of extravagantly dressed dandies known as sapeurs, is famous in Brazzaville. Food is based on cassava, fish, plantains and saka-saka (cassava leaves).

politics.heading: Dominant presidency
paragraphs: Congo is a presidential republic in which President Denis Sassou Nguesso and his Congolese Party of Labour have dominated for decades. A 2015 constitutional referendum removed age and term limits. Elections are criticised by the opposition and observers, and dissent is restricted.

economy.heading: Oil economy
paragraphs: Oil, mostly offshore, provides the majority of exports and government revenue, making Congo one of sub-Saharan Africa's largest oil producers. Timber from its rainforests, which are part of the Congo Basin, the world's second-largest tropical forest, is also important.
Despite this, much of the population lives in poverty, and the country has faced debt crises. The currency is the Central African CFA franc.
